utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read aloud the affirmation that's on the card that's shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. I should mention, Mr. Lukic, that Judge Thelin finds himself not able to sit. We expect he will be able to sit on Monday, and we'll continue to sit under the Rule today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Stojic. On behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin, I shall be asking you questions. I told you during our proofing to try and make a pause between my question and your answer because we understand each other. But in order to obtain an adequate interpretation, it is necessary for the interpreters to interpret every word of ours. I shall, likewise, on my part, wait for the end of your answer before asking my next question. We know that you speak English well, and you will probably be understanding the questions posed to you by the Prosecutor; but please also wait in that case, because we want that to be fully recorded in the transcript. Can we first have your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I am now going to go through your CV, your career, and your biography, which is quite extensive and very prominent. But I shall try to inform the Trial Chamber about the important elements in your career, which I think are of relevance to appreciate your role and your place in terms of the facts that we are going to be discussing here. So you were born in 1938, in the town of Uzice, in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You completed high military schools in the military realm; and also, as a civilian, you completed different degrees of schooling in different universities. So I should now like to deal with the military schools first. You completed the Ground Forces Military Academy, 1959; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then the Command Staff School in 1965.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The School of National Defence as the highest military school of in the then JNA.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in parallel with this education, obviously your ambition did not end with the military schooling, so that after high school you also obtained a law degree in 1968, in which year you graduated from the law school, law faculty, in Split.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then in Belgrade you obtained a master's degree at the Political Sciences Faculty in 1977.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, you obtained your Ph.D. also at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade in 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your career, you published a number of papers on international relations; and you are currently director, that is to say, after retiring in 1994, you were - and I'm not quite sure whether you are still that - director for the Institute for Geopolitical Studies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No. I'm just a member of the executive board for the Institute for Geopolitical Studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the time which is of relevance to us, in 1991, you were a colonel in the Yugoslav People's Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me not go through all the promotions to the different ranks, because what we are concerned with is the relevant period. So you had a traditional career/promotion line, but you had an accelerated promotion into the rank of lieutenant colonel, which you also told us yesterday, in the presence of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you retired in 1994, in which year you became a general major -- major general; and in that rank, you were actually retired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another interesting element in your career, generally speaking in its military component, is that you were quite linked with the military intelligence service; namely, in the segment of its international relations or its diplomatic relations. Have I defined that properly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also were a lecturer at high military schools for a while, the subject being international political relations and intelligence matters, I suppose; and you were prepared for and were supposed to assume the post of military attache in Chile. And because of the circumstances we are familiar with, after the death of Allende and when Yugoslavia broke off diplomatic relations with Chile, that didn't actually materialise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you were also to be a military attache in London, which post was held by Mr. Brovet, Admiral Brovet, who was later your superior in the relevant period; and interestingly enough, for a number of years, five or six, I believe, you were the military representative; i.e., the representative of the JNA in Iraq during the vehement Iraq-Iran war, when you our the military attache in Iraq and Iran, and in the Middle East, in general.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Not in Iraq; in Tehran, Iran.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you were the Assistant Chief of General Staff for International Relations for the Asia and Africa region. Have I got that well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Not exactly. I was in the intelligence administration, in charge of the Africa and Asia sector; and that is approximately that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At a certain point in time, in 1988 up to 1994, meaning also in the period that we are going to deal with today, you were the chief of administration for liaison with foreign military representations attached to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we are now talking about the relevant period, will you tell us what was the duty of this administration, and who were you directly subordinated to at that time? Of course, we're interested, as you well know yourself, in 1991 specifically. But generally, what were -- what work did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: The basic task of this administration, which also comprises a liaison office to liaise with diplomatic and military representations; and legations was to plan and implement inter-army cooperation, to establish relations with military diplomatic and diplomatic representatives, and to also carry out protocol security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the activities of your department in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: The situation had changed, so that instead of our activities in inter-army cooperation, we actually focused in our work on protocol security; reception and seeing off, ensuring interpretation for foreign and military diplomatic representatives who sought to influence, i.e., contribute to the finding of a peaceful solution of the crisis in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior? To whom were you, as an administration and you personally, subordinated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I was directly subordinated to general of the army, Veljko Kadijevic. But between me and the army general, at that time, the federal secretary for national defence was his deputy, Admiral Stane Brovet. It was only in exceptional cases that I addressed directly the Army General Kadijevic. Otherwise, all other contacts would be established through his deputy, Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I failed to ask you this in connection with your career, and it can be of relevance for your further testimony: What was your knowledge of the English language like at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Professors say that my English was good. I think that it was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your liaisons with foreign persons that you got in touch with, did you have an interpreter, or could you directly, personally, communicate with those people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: It was always me personally talking; and if there was an activity that involved the participation of other people, then I would have an interpreter sent to interpret from the services within my administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Trial Chamber, when you say "protocol security," "protocol support," what does that comprise in lay terms? What are those?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, if somebody is appointed to a specific duty which actually implies an agreement, then we receive such letters. We then refer them to the competent people for their assessment. And in addition to that, as I said initially, we assist in protocol matters, in liaison matters, and assist them in all such activities. But, as I also said, in the beginning of 1991, we rather were engaged on protocol area support than the actual planning of activities. So that meant receiving, seeing off, accommodating guests, seeing to their security. That was number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, in November, did you have a specific task, or did you have any mission in the region of Vukovar? Can you tell us; and if you remember the date, when was that? Who was that mission given to you by?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of November, 1991, Admiral Brovet called me and he ordered me to put myself at the disposal of the envoy of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. Cyrus Vance, with his delegation, who wanted to tour parts of Vukovar and the units that were engaged there. I do not remember exactly whether it was during working hours. At that time we used to work all day, as a rule, but I know that it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he give you any guidelines in respect to this visit; what you particularly needed to focus on, or was this just information that they would be going and was that just it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: He gave me a very specific assignment, in which it said that I should receive the guests, welcome them on the following day, that is to say, on the 19th, at 7.00; then, that I should take them to the area of Vukovar, and that I should pay particular attention to their safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're moving on to the morning of the 19th. Do you remember who was on that delegation? How many members it had?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I could not give you the names of all the members of the delegation, but I do remember some of them. And I will try to tell you now. The head of the delegation was His Excellency Mr. Cyrus Vance, as Special Envoy of the Secretary-General of the United Nations. General Marrack Goulding was also as Under Secretary for Political Affairs in the United Nations. I remember Colonel Purola, perhaps more than the others, because we had the same rank. And I also remember Ambassador Okun. That is four altogether. There were another four members of the delegation. The other day when I spoke to you, I saw my report and their names and exact positions are listed there. I can't remember everything because, after all, it's been 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's quite understandable. I did not want you to really do all of that, but I just wanted to see what your recollection was. Was this your first meeting with Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see him on other occasions; and if so, do you remember where and when?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Another three or four times. I cannot be very specific on that, but that was our first meeting. After that, a few other times, three or four. All of that within the next five or ten days; that is to say, after the visit to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are seeking fact testimony here, but what was your impression of Mr. Vance at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: An exceptional man; very fair, very objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you depart from Belgrade, and where did you go first, if you remember? Did you go somewhere else before you went to Vukovar? If you can tell us roughly what the time was, but I don't insist on that at all.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I have an excellent recollection of some things; whereas, as far as some other things are concerned, what I saw in your office the other day and a year and a half ago on television, so all of it put together, I do have a general picture of this entire visit, from when it began until when it ended. We left Belgrade around 7.00 in the morning, because on that day we were supposed to return as early as possible, by 1500 hours, 1530 hours, because the plan was for His Excellency, Mr. Cyrus Vance, to travel to go Zagreb for talks with the president of Croatia, Dr. Tudjman. We left Belgrade and went towards Sid. Sid was supposed to be the first stop on this working visit. We arrived around ten to 8.00, just before 8.00. That's when we arrived at Sid. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you travel to Sid?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: By cars. I was in the second car with Mr. Cyrus Vance in order to be able to answer all his questions, all the questions that he put during the course of the journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how much time you spent in Sid? How long that visit lasted, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly how long it lasted. I think it was about 40 minutes, less than an hour. We had talks there. Should I explain what we did there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't really want to dwell on that very long, but just what happened in Sid before you continued your journey, in the sense of your transport, how you travelled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When we ended our visit there, and our host there was the president of the municipal assembly of Sid, his name was Mr. Popovic. I had forgotten his first name, but I saw in your documents that it was Mr. Jovan Popovic. Then we were supposed to continue our journey to Vukovar. However, I was surprised when I saw that there were APCs waiting for us in front of the municipal assembly; and when a warrant officer told us- I don't know his name- that due to security reasons, we had to continue our journey on APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you react to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Since Admiral Brovet ordered me that in case of anything unplanned happening I should notify him straight away, I started thinking as to whether we should continue our journey at all. Because I was thinking, how can such a high level dignitary and a delegation like that be put into armoured personnel carriers; how can I take them somewhere as be put into armoured personnel carriers; how can I take them somewhere as if we were some wartime unit. I called Admiral Brovet and I asked him to tell me what the position was. Should we continue our journey or should we go back? Admiral Brovet told me that I should judge it myself and talk to the persons involved in providing security there. I asked this warrant officer, who was at the head of two APCs, whether it was necessary to take such vehicles and why we were doing that. And he said to me that there was a likelihood of sniper shooters. The journey was supposed to take place through a forest, and these sniper shooters could open fire at the convoy. I told Mr. Vance about that, and I asked him to decide as well. I conveyed to him the content of my discussion with Admiral Brovet. He asked me what the situation was at the command post in Negoslavci, because this was the second stop on our work visit. I was told that this area around the command post was secured, that this was carried out by the security organs and security details. So we agreed that we should continue our journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you actually board the APCs, and did you actually take these APCs to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now we are going to watch a brief videoclip, V0001128. That is a document that was already admitted into evidence as an exhibit, so you will see it on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can comment on this, Mr. Stojic. What is it we're seeing now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: A convoy of vehicles departing from Belgrade and going to Sid. Now we've arrived in Sid and we are getting out. The president of the municipal assembly, Popovic, greeting Mr. Cyrus Vance. I'm right behind him. Do you see? In uniform, a colonel's uniform. I just don't have my cap on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you the man who is holding his hat and his coat in his hands?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Precisely. And right behind me, there is a lieutenant colonel in uniform, with a cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: You can see me better now. On the right, the man to the right of Cyrus Vance, Jovan Popovic, the interpreter who worked in my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is wearing a grey jacket; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I am right behind him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can no longer hear the proceedings in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I am now helping him enter the vehicle. You can see my rank insignia, but my hair is dark. It's been 15 years, after all. Now I'm sitting in the APC, together with Mr. Cyrus Vance, who insisted that I should be with him all the time and that I should assist him, explain to him things that he sees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've stopped the videoclip because -- well, Your Honours, can we please get a number for this videoclip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the first part, but the exhibit started from the moment when they arrive in Negoslavci, if you remember. I can check during the break, but my colleague tells me that she already did check. The exhibit starts from when the arrived in Negoslavci. We are going to watch that, too. But this is the preceding part of the TV report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it all one video? I think we will simply record that the whole of the video is now comprising the exhibit, and perhaps the court officer could remind us of the number. Perhaps you might be able to remind us, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague, Ms. Dokmanovic, told me that that it's Exhibit 74 -- Exhibit 70, rather, that it starts from the sequel to this. But we don't have this particular footage in that. However, all of it was dealt with in the 65 ter documents, the entire report. However, in Exhibit 70, we haven't got this. The Prosecution actually tendered a different part when Mr. Okun testified as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole video is now Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, where did you go after Sid? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: After Sid, we went to the village of Negoslavci, which is 33 kilometres away from Sid. That is where the command post was of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody receive you there? Did you have a meeting there, and what happened during such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: On arrival in front of the building, in which the command post of the Operations Group South was, we were met by the commander of the group, Colonel -- at that time, Colonel Mrksic. And he took us into the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anything specific that transpired in the operations room, or rather, relay the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: In the operations room, we stayed for around 30 to 35 minutes. During that time, the commander, Colonel Mrksic, informed us about the situation in that part of the front or in that region. In front of us there was a map which we, in the military, call a war map, in which were inscribed elements of the combat disposition and the line of demarcation. Colonel Mrksic explained to us that the zone of responsibility of his operations group, in depth, was the River Vuka; and he also indicated another two points on the right and left boundaries -- I don't now remember whether it was the village of Tovarnik, or something like that, but I know that the in-depth point was the River Vuka. On that occasion, he told me that across the River Vuka, the zone of responsibility was that of Operations Group North. He also gave us a number of other details which I truly could not recall in their entirety now. After 30 to 35 minutes, Colonel Mrksic called Major Veselin Sljivancanin and told him that he would be our host, responsible for the further course of the visit while we stayed in his zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, do approach the microphones and relax in your chair.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: After that, we set out to the barracks, if I can call it a barracks, because it was a building riddled with bullets. It was destroyed. It had many traces of combat operations as, after all, the whole of Vukovar had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us who was in the delegation. Do you remember which officer accompanied you as you proceeded in your visit to Vukovar? You said that Mr. Sljivancanin was with you. Were there any other officers with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of them, but I could only recall the names of two. One of them was, at that time, Colonel Pavkovic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, who otherwise is not organically within the composition of the unit commanded by Colonel Mrksic. And we also had Lieutenant Colonel Djukic with us, who was from the cabinet. He was a security officer, and he was practically in charge of us, and that charge was given to him by the Federal Secretary of National Defence. As for the two or three lower-ranking officers, I wouldn't be able, right now, to say anything specific about them. I believe that they were there with a number of men, a number of soldiers, who accompanied us throughout the visit to ensure our security. I believe that they belonged to Colonel Mrksic's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, in respect of these officers whom you mentioned, whether they were with you throughout your visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: You mean Colonel Pavkovic and Lieutenant Colonel Djukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you at the beginning, but let me ask you: Were you there throughout the visit of Mr. Cyrus Vance? Were you with him or by him all that time, at his side throughout the visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: During the actual journey, I sat by him in the car, next to him. During the tour of the city, I was some four or five metres behind or around him, because I gave way to the host. I stepped back a couple of metres in order to keep tabs on the situation, which is actually the way it should have been, according to protocol. But, basically, I was with His Excellency, Mr. Cyrus Vance, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this further tour of Vukovar and the points that you stopped at, who was the person who was the most engaged in talking with Mr. Vance? Who was his host in that part of the visit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the barracks, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to give you a precise answer; ten to 15 minutes, I believe. But not in the barracks proper, we were in the compound, in the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall be looking at the footage shortly. Do you recall whether Mr. Vance asked to see the Vukovar Hospital; and if so, when did he make that request, and what happened in response to it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: During the talks in the barracks compound, around the time when we were about to leave, Mr. Vance asked Major Sljivancanin if there existed a possibility for the Vukovar Hospital to be also seen. That was the first time a reference to the hospital was made. Major Sljivancanin replied that it was his opinion that within the brief time at our disposal, for security considerations, it was impossible to organise such a visit. And I think, I'm not quite certain, I think that he also mentioned seeing that the hospital is across the River Vuka in the zone of the Operations Group North. I believe that he uttered a comment to the effect that it was some four or five kilometres away from the place where we were, and that the hospital was in the center of town. So, actually, he said that it was his opinion that it was impossible to ensure that within a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this dialogue, which you have just now related to us, did anyone, Mr. Brovet or Mr. Vance or anyone else, mention to you their desire to make this visit to the Vukovar Hospital? I mean before this dialogue.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were issued this task by Brovet, was it your job to make an itinerary of all the working stops that you would be making in such a visit? Was that your task?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of the plans for such a visit envisage a visit to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened afterwards? What was the reaction after this dialogue between Mr. Vance and Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vance inquired whether, after all, there did exist some possibility for him to visit the Vukovar Hospital, whether there was someone who ensure that, probably meaning someone from the Operations Group North. The answer that was given him was that at that moment, and given the shortness of time, it was impossible to ensure appropriate security, and that it would be taking a risk to set off into the unknown, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in any way in this dialogue or in any talks on this topic? Did you participate, and did you react to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I approached. I walked up to them and I asked in a very small voice, Pavkovic and Djukic, what they thought about it. They also were of the view that it would be highly risky, because this was not a group of journalists who would be taking that risk of their own accord, but this was a delegation of the United Nations, a high-ranking United Nations delegation. Then I approached Mr. Sljivancanin and I asked him, in a very low voice, whether there did, after all, exist some possibility, and he just shrugged his shoulders. And then I made the decision to ask Mr. Vance, if he should insist to go to the hospital, in that case, I decided that I would call Admiral Brovet and ask them for their position on the issue. Only a higher ranking -- the higher ranking superior command could have brought a decision. That is the way it goes, according to military hierarchy. That is the line of command and control. However, that proved to be unnecessary. I did not have to call Admiral Brovet. I walked up to Mr. Vance, and I only told him that it was my opinion that we should not be taking that risk; and he acquiesced, and that was the end of it. No one mentioned the Vukovar Hospital ever, any more. And I assert, with responsibility, that that was the first time that I heard about that hospital, and that I was not actually familiar with the details of the situation on that part of the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit 70. But before that, Your Honours, can I kindly ask you to -- while this video footage is played, can you look at the transcripts, which you still have before you, which are the MFI transcripts, because the Defence feels that the transcript is not faithfully and completely translated. But I should like to ask you to follow. It is not a question of translation, actually; but when it was transcribed, some things have been omitted. So if you could please be so kind as to do that. Can I ask the usher to give the Trial Chamber these copies, so that we can follow this particular footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do the interpreters have a copy, Mr. Lukic? Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution can assist. We prepared a revised transcript and translation of this video, which I believe was sent to my learned friend. I don't know if he's had a chance to fully check that. The Prosecution has made copies for distribution in court this morning; and if my friend would like, perhaps that can be distributed and allay his fears about the MFI transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lunny says they've had the earlier transcript revised, so there's an improved version. It might be useful if we look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is what I got from the OTP. What I received some two or three weeks ago from the OTP, as they say, the revised version, that is the version marked V0001231.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If Mr. Lukic could kindly slow down with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is the version, that is the one I'm handing over right now, unless he's talking about a more recent one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny, perhaps the Chamber could have the revised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. That is the revised one. I see it's not really helping with my learned friend's fears, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He's perhaps not had a chance to study it yet, and is there a copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it has been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They seem to be the same, Mr. Lukic, from what I've been able to see so far. You've distributed the revised one, and Mr. Lunny has given us a duplicate copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I apologise for the confusion and the waste of the court time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's nobody's fault in particular, Mr. Lunny, but we may soon see the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me draw your attention to something. I don't want it to have anything to do with Mr. Stojic's testimony. Your Honours, please pay attention to the transcript when you read it and when you watch the video footage. Please look at page 2, pay attention to that, lines 14 to 22 in English on page 2. The B/C/S transcript and the English transcript have something there -- well, I'm not going to say anything now, because the witness is here. But that is what remains controversial from the time when Mr. Okun gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see this on your screen, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Arrival and entering the operations room. This is the welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we go further, Mr. Lukic, we are not getting English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Interpreters note: That part that is not transcribed, and we do not have the text. The original soundtrack is much too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a news commentary. What we have heard so far in B/C/S is commentary by the journalist. That was not relevant to us, so we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Let us take a walk around the compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see Colonel Pavkovic here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Soldiers and commanding officers of all peoples of Yugoslavia are here /unintelligible/ more than 18 year old.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot read the transcript and interpret court proceedings at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Before the Yugoslav People's Army units liberated Vukovar, some 400-500 mortar missiles were being launched on our barracks daily. When we imprisoned the rest of the Ustasha soldiers and the second part of the citizens last night, I was proud of my soldiers who never tried even for a moment to take revenge on anybody, but they helped them as much as it was needed. We teach and train all our soldiers and commanding officers that it is very much humane and a great honour to help every man and every people. Also, sir, this here is one dirty war that has never in history been waged this way. The Yugoslav army, the Yugoslav People's Army originates from the army that fought fascism in the Second World War along with the other allies. No, our soldiers had all taken part, along with us the positions, in performing... in liberating the city of Vukovar. I think I cannot ensure that at the moment. There is safe passage. He can solve that because in there, where the passage across the Vuka River is located, between us and this "North" Operations Group, there are minefields and we are not prepared to take you where you won't be safe. We still haven't cleared these minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, during your proofing, we watched this video footage. Do you remember whether you were present during this dialogue? Is that the way you recall that this took place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I was four or five metres away from Mr. Cyrus Vance and Major Sljivancanin. I listened to every word, and right now I can say to you that my teacher did not interpret everything perfectly. Major Sljivancanin said, "I think that in this short period of time, we could not ensure a trip to the Vukovar Hospital," and Professor Jovan Jeremic, my teacher, the interpreter said "I cannot," whereas, what he said was "we cannot." As they were talking, I slowly approached Colonel Pavkovic and Lieutenant Colonel Djukic and asked them what they thought. This is the first time I heard of this hospital. You must understand me, my task was to take care of the delegation. And if I just say that I travelled on APCs from Sid to Negoslavci; and then, now, all of a sudden they go out into an open area into the center of town, I mean this is the first time I've heard of all this. This was, well, a moment when I needed to consult my superior command, or rather, Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You explained that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I wanted to note that the interpretation heard on the video is not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have another interpretation here. Don't worry about that. As this conversation was taking place, do you remember whether Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Djukic were nearby?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Two metres away or one metre away, right behind Mr. Cyrus Vance and Major Sljivancanin. And I am next to them, except that I'm trying to stay out of the way because I'm not the host at that point, but I'm following everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going to ask the witness anything else in relation to this subject, but I would kindly ask that we view once again this part that I find controversial. It is at 2:18, roughly, when Mr. Vance is putting this question. "See if we can make arrangements with the people of the Northern Command to see the hospital." That is on page 2, from line 12. And then after that, you will hear what I kept objecting to, that an unknown voice says, "No, no," and only then Mr. Sljivancanin gives his answer. Your Honours, please pay attention to Mr. Sljivancanin's face at that point. So it's somebody else who is saying, "No, no," and then the translation that was provided here says, "There is a secure passage." We claim that the unknown voice is saying, "There is no secure passage." Please have a look. This is what we have been trying to work out with the Prosecution and the CLSS for over a year now. I'm not going to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I think that right now I cannot provide for that. That can be resolved because where the passage where the Vuka is located, between us and this north operations group, there are minefields, and we are not prepared to take you where you won't be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask that you leave us some more time. I can talk to our friends from the OTP, that we and the Prosecutors look at this together with the interpreters so that, by next Friday, we inform you what we all hear, whether they agree with what we, the Defence, hear in that particular clip. We are not challenging anything else, but let us see if we can finally all agree on what is actually heard in that clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it your submission, Mr. Lukic, that this voice saying, "No, no," that you hear is relevant to the conversation between your client and Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that is exactly what I think. I've viewed it several times with this witness. We see who is on the film. But in view of the first transcript and the assertion made by the OTP that my client is the person who decides that Mr. Vance cannot travel to the hospital, it is relevant for me that there is this other voice saying, "No, no," and that there is another voice that says there is not a secure or safe passage there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If it can be resolved between the parties, that will be fine. Otherwise, the Chamber will have to assess the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Stojic, where were you after the barracks, and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: After the compound of the barracks, we went to a facility that is called Velepromet that was used as a holding centre for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the details? What happened there? How long did you stay there? What is it you recall from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you a great deal about this, especially as far as details are concerned. After all, it's been 15 years. But I know that there were some warehouses there, that many people were in front of these buildings - women, children, elderly persons. I also saw some people, a few people, in uniform. This uniform was different from what members of Operations Group South wore. I mean, this was attire that was no longer used. I also saw a few soldiers who belonged to the unit of Colonel Mrksic. I think they were people from security. Because throughout our stay there, and as we were moving about at different working points, the security was checking the area. Mr. Cyrus Vance was engaged in talks there. There was a person there in uniform; I don't know what his name was. He was in charge of this centre. I don't even know what his official title was. Was that director or commander or commanding officer? At any rate, all of that went on for ten or 15 minutes, not more than that. Perhaps it was a bit more, but I cannot be very accurate now and I cannot tell you exactly. Well, that is what I could say to you at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go down to the center of town? Do you remember that you were ever on a square in the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No. We were not at any square. That would have been dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does Milovo Brdo mean anything to you? Did you, perhaps, go to some elevation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I did not know about that until the other evening, when you told me what the name was. But we did climb up there and we watched Vukovar a bit from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: After that we went to the hospital in the village of Negoslavci. Well, not exactly in the village. It's a bit on the outskirts of the village. But that is the hospital that took in the wounded and the ill. It belonged to the army or to the 5th Operations Group. I cannot remember exactly now. I knew everything then, but now, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At all these points that we described now, how did you move about in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: On APCs. The seat where I sat otherwise, next to Mr. Cyrus Vance, in order to be able to talk to him, was taken by Major Sljivancanin. I ordered the interpreter to be in a position that would enable communication with Mr. Vance; that is to say, Mr. Sljivancanin and Major Vance -- Major Sljivancanin and Mr. Vance. So I was a bit further away. I was in the third row compared to them. That is what the APC looks like. There are eight seats, and the driver and the co-driver, so that's a total of eight seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Sljivancanin in that vehicle when you went from Vukovar to the Negoslavci hospital? And what was he doing in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I've been telling you about. Major Sljivancanin sat in the seat in the APC that I sat in before that, on the trip from Sid to Vukovar. He was talking to Mr. Vance. But I could not follow that conversation, because it is impossible without a headset in an APC. I would just like to tell the honourable Trial Chamber that even communication between the driver and co-driver requires the use of a headset because of the noise levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Visually, what did this dialogue between the two of them seem like to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Perfectly normal. I really don't know what you mean. They were talking without any gesticulation, perfectly normally, the way people talk, the way two interlocutors would engage in a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking you this. Mr. Stojic, throughout the visit - I'm going to ask you this yet again - from the moment you arrived in Vukovar and throughout the visit, until you left Negoslavci, were you near Mr. Vance and Sljivancanin all the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it also your duty to follow the entire course of the visit and the conduct of Mr. Vance and his collocutors?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But I have to mention that I was ordered, and that is indeed the practice, to follow everything that was happening; who was doing what, who was in charge of what, who was responsible for what, and to put that in a report in order for my superiors to be able to take the necessary, appropriate, measures; that is to say, if something was remiss, for that something to be rectified, and in order for us to know what further steps to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall be coming to that report. But tell me at this point, did you see at any point during the visit that there was emotions running high, or there was a more vehement discussion between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Vance? Were there any raised voices?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, an even stranger question: Did you see at any moment Mr. Sljivancanin point a rifle or any kind of weapon at Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any journalists there during your visit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Throughout the visit, there were representatives of the mass media with us, both from our country as well as foreign journalists, and TV crews, correspondents. Actually, they were very eager to come near and hear what the conversation was being -- was about in order to report back to their agencies and to their houses, and film the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone prohibited the journalists from filming anything or recording anything throughout the visit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. It was desirable for them to record what they heard and saw and report it back to their agencies and houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you -- how much time did you spend at the hospital in Negoslavci, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That was where we spent the most time among all the working stops. Between 45 and 50 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, when you said goodbye to Mr. Vance, I mean when you, your delegation, and Mr. Vance parted and he said goodbye to Mr. Sljivancanin, what was that like?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They said goodbye at the exit from the hospital compound. They shook hands quite normally, as did all the other members of the delegation. They also said goodbye to Major Sljivancanin. Colonel Purola uttered a comment which I didn't pay any attention to. It was probably some courtesy comment. I didn't get it. Then we got on the APCs, and Mr. Cyrus Vance, again, asked me to sit by him so that we could comment the just-finished visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have seen your report which we will be analysed a bit later and which has probably jogged your memories. But tell me, do you remember what you talked about with Mr. Vance on your way to Belgrade? While you were returning to Belgrade, what were his words?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I remember -- I remember, and what I consider to be of importance I have inserted in my report, which I wrote the very same night upon arrival in Belgrade, and with permission from this honourable Trial Chamber I can highlight a couple of the sentences exchanged during the conversation, some segments of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us that in a couple of words. Then we shall put the report itself in front of you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he also used to be an active officer, a frigate captain, as far as I remember, it was not difficult for him to actually recognise everything that is characteristic of a military unit. He said that he had gained the impression that the unit, i.e., the men, members, of the unit of Operations Group South, that they were disciplined, that they had a proper appearance, soldierly appearance, in line, in array, that is, starting with their posture up to their uniforms and their bearing. And he also had a comment to the effect that -- which referred to all the peoples in the former Yugoslavia, and this is more or less what he said: Yugoslavs, so not Serbs, not Muslims, not Macedonians; he said, Yugoslavs are militant and courageous people, but he also said that they will take up arms very easily and also be very trigger-happy, which is very dangerous if they are led by nationalist leaders. He said something along those lines. He also said that he observed, as a lesser problem, he said that he observed that a lesser problem, the blocking of the barracks, can produce, can generate, a major problem which can escalate into a conflict. And this is his comment and his conclusion after touring the barracks in Vukovar. And he added that, in relation to that particular subject, he would be talking with Dr. Tudjman, the President of Croatia, that very same day. And he also said, and he was bothered by the fact that we saw approaching the barracks, not in the compound, but right there. In the immediate vicinity, we saw a number of members of the armed forces, not from Colonel Mrksic's unit, who exuded an air which was not soldierly, as we would put it, because of the way they were dressed, because of the way they were comporting themselves. They were hanging around, I could say. And this is what he was bothered by. And he told me that on that account he would be talking to General Kadijevic and Admiral Brovet, and that I should also relay this to this; namely, that these people needed to be put under the control of the regular army as soon as possible. And he may have said some other things that I might remember if I consulted my report, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the first witness with whom I have overstepped my time limit. I do have two more brief topics. I believe it is, however, now time for our break. I believe that we shall all be expeditious with Mr. Stojic today so that we shall end in time. I just wish to deal with this report a bit later, after the break, to complete -- to wrap up this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're right that we must now have the first break. The tape's nearly run out. So we will resume at five minutes to the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, can you tell us, approximately, when you returned to Belgrade on that day, with that delegation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Around 1530 hours, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the next time you saw Mr. Vance? And where was this, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I think it was already on the following day, when I went to pick him up at the hotel, and I took him to the building of the Federal Secretariate for National Defence for a meeting with General Kadijevic and his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who else was present at the meeting, in addition to Mr. Vance and Mr. Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Should I mention all the names? Admiral Brovet, General Jovic, Colonel Vuk Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone from Mr. Vance's delegation who attended the meeting as well? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that Mr. Goulding was there; then Mr. Okun, Colonel Purola, and two other persons from the remaining four. Six out of eight, which was the total number of members of this delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the subject of the conversation was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. Should I proceed? General Kadijevic had his report in front of him, my report on the visit. Also, Admiral Brovet and General Jovic and Colonel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said, "Obradovic" before.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I do beg your pardon. I meant Obradovic. The general asked Mr. Cyrus Vance - General Kadijevic asked, that is - to tell him about his impressions of the visit. Not waiting for his answer, the general gave an introduction. He talked about the situation as it was. And after he finished, Mr. Cyrus Vance spoke. I do not remember the details, but I know that Mr. Cyrus Vance gave his impressions briefly. He mostly spoke about the content of the talk he had with Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the President of Croatia. Right now, I really could not tell you more about the content of that conversation. I was there for the sake of protocol. I was not a participant in the talks. I was basically in charge of protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at that time there were any objections raised by Mr. Cyrus Vance in respect of his visit to Vukovar, any objections against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: There weren't any objections raised against the JNA on the part of Mr. Cyrus Vance, but he did note that he saw armed people who should be placed under the control of the operative units of the JNA as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was the relationship like between General Kadijevic and Mr. Vance? How did you view it? How many times did they meet in your presence, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, four times. I was always present, and I can tell you that the relationship was more than friendly. I also have to note that General Kadijevic graduated from high military schools in the United States; and since they were roughly the same age, or of a similar age, it is possible that they knew each other from before. I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any other details in terms of some particular attentiveness between the two of them? If so, could you please tell us about that, just in a few words.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the meeting was over, in the operations room of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, General Kadijevic beckoned to me and told me to prepare a present for Mr. Cyrus Vance, which was the general custom as far as such guests were concerned, guests who were accorded special attention. He ordered me to prepare a pistol, manufactured by the Crvena Zastava arms factory in Kragojevac; and that I should also prepare a small plaque with an inscription by way of a dedication. I did that, of course. I cannot give you an exact answer now as to whether it was on the following day or two days later. General Kadijevic already had health problems at that time. He was about to undergo surgery at the Military Medical Academy. So, as I said, a day or two later we went to the Military Medical Academy; Mr. Cyrus Vance, Mr. Okun, and Colonel Purola. I don't know whether there was a fourth person there, too. We paid a visit to General Kadijevic. In the suite where he was staying at the Military Medical Academy, they had a friendly meeting; and at the end of that meeting, General Kadijevic presented this gift to His Excellency, Mr. Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't be dealing with that any long. But during your dealings after Vukovar, did Mr. Vance, Mr. Okun, anyone from that delegation, present any criticism to you personal live on account of that visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No. May I just say something else? I organised a dinner for the entire delegation in the army centre of the JNA. All the persons are mentioned in the report. I don't want to go through that yet again. At that dinner various subjects were discussed, but we no longer mentioned the visit to Vukovar, nor was anything referred to in relation to that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see document 3D05-0387. We received this document from the OTP this summer, I think, according to Rule 68, but I'm not sure now. Can we just see the letterhead first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, tell us, what is this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: This is the report that I wrote during the night between the 19th and 20th of November, upon my return from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this report pertain to what you testified about today?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just see the last page of this report on our screens, please, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you submit this report to? Who were copies sent to, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: To the cabinet, the office of the Federal Secretary for National Defence; to the cabinet, office of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the SFRY, that was the previous Yugoslavia; the Deputy, Federal Secretary for National Defence, Admiral Brovet; the Department for Moral Guidance of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence; the Security Administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence; and the 2nd Administration of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, the Intelligence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for this report, is that the one that Mr. Kadijevic, Mr. Brovet, and Mr. Obradovic had before them, prior to the meeting with Mr. Vance that you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that the report is self-explanatory. I have no questions in relation to that. Mr. Stojic, I have concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would just like to ask this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 861, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stojic. I am Vladimir Domazet, Attorney at Law; one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic. I am going to put a few questions to you. Mr. Stojic, in view of what you have told us, referring to your participation in the talks with Mr. Vance and in escorting him, I should like you to tell us whether in these talks, or in any other way, you learned what the position was of Mr. Vance, as a UN envoy, in relation to a resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, which pertained at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vance's position was that efforts should be exerted in order for the earliest possible deblocking of the military barracks and towards finding a negotiated solution in order to put an end to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be it in the most succinct, briefest terms. Do you know what the European Monitoring Mission's position was at the time, and were there any differences between the stance of that mission and what Mr. Vance was doing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I could not give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojic, when you came to the command of OG South at Negoslavci, you mentioned today that there was a map, a war map, as you said, in which were certainly inscribed the operations and the situation. I should like to know whether the map that you saw was updated up to the 19th of November, in terms of the operations that had been drawn in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I could not see the date, and I can only suppose that it was. But I could not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But according to what was said at the time - probably, there were explanations being given of what was in the map - was it said that the operations in Vukovar had been completed and that there were no more combat operations, or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, they said that there were no more operations. But we don't refer to them as operations, we say "combat." But they said that the entire city, the entire territory, had not been cleaned yet. That is what I remember. I could not give you any more detailed comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you had a prepared plan of activities, an itinerary for the visit. I suppose that was also discussed at Negoslavci when you were received by Commander Mrksic. My question is whether he had any objections to the plan or comments in relation to it. Were there any restrictions being imposed on you, on any elements of your planned visit, or, on the contrary, were you told that they could see everything that they wanted to see?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: The position was that they should be shown everything that they wished to see, and that we would hide nothing from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you were quite decided in your answer to a similar question by my colleague Lukic, as regards the raising of the matter of the visit to the hospital for the first time, but I shall ask you anyway. During this meeting at the command of the operations group, in the presence of Commander Mrksic, was a visit to the hospital at all raised? Was the question of the possibility of visiting the hospital raised at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago you had in front of you, your own report which you compiled and submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps it would be good for us to see the last page on our screens again. That is Exhibit 861, the one that has just been tendered. Can we zoom in and scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, would you please be so kind as to read out the last sentence, which is just above, "Report drawn up by Colonel M.A. Petar Stojic."

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The last sentence contained my own assessment, which was based on my talks with His Excellency, Mr. Cyrus Vance and members of the delegation, and it is that the visit was very successful; and to that I added, on my part, that is, my own contribution, to which the greatest contribution was rendered by the command of the Operations Group South. Can I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: From Sid, up to the time we returned again to Sid, we were accompanied at all times by security elements. And because of the very fact that the command had made this assessment, seeing that we were to travel through wooded areas, that there was a possibility for a sniper to open fire at the guests, and because -- also because it was possible for the delegation to see at every moment what was possibly to be seen, generally speaking, it was my assessment that the command of OG South could have done nothing more than that for the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. Thank you for your answers. Just another question related to the Negoslavci meeting chaired by Commander Mrksic. Can you tell me, in the briefest of terms, what kind of an atmosphere prevailed? Was it tense? Was it relaxed? Was it good? What was your assessment of the overall atmosphere of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere was soldierly in the true sense of the word. Only very concrete matters were discussed. The map showed a lot. One could, in particular, see on it the zone of responsibility of the Operations Group South, which was extremely important for Colonel Purola, the military advisor. So they spoke in very specific terms. We followed an agenda with items spelled out beforehand, and I didn't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If Your Honour would allow me a moment just to set up the lectern. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to Vukovar in the autumn of 1991, September, October, and November of 1991, the war in Vukovar, the battle in Vukovar, was major news, wasn't it? It was a big event in the former Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that it was major news, that it was breaking news. I am not quite certain, but the idea was that it should be stopped and that a solution should be found without using force, in order to protect the constitutional order. Now, whether Vukovar was the major news amid that, I was rather engaged in diplomatic work and I did not participate in operative meetings or contribute to such assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But you were involved in diplomatic work. You're a soldier. There was fighting going on in your country. You would have been watching the news every night on television when you got the chance, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: When I had the opportunity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the daily news in Belgrade covered the fighting in Vukovar, and we've seen videos today showing the press at Belgrade -- sorry, at Vukovar, certainly for your trip; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And not only was the national press taking an interest in the events in Vukovar, so, too, was the international media. The BBC was there; SkyNews was there. Isn't that also true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That is true. That is true. And all the events were covered by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And this national and international press that had been following Vukovar through September, October, November 1991, was also following what was happening at the hospital, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: It probably was, but I'm here to describe what happened on the 19th. As for what happened before or after that, I can only give you a general description. But if you ask me about that particular day, the 19th, the 20th, i.e., the 18th, 19th and 20th, in addition to what I have put in my report, I can give you a number of other answers to the best of my recollection. In September and October 1991, and then the end of November and December 1991 and in 1992, all I know about is what happened in that period is a bit more than an ordinary citizen or an ordinary member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So is it your position -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: If I can add, I have been called here as a Defence witness to say what I know about the visit, that visit to Vukovar. As regards your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can stop you there, Mr. Stojic. We know you're here to discuss a specific event, but I'm asking you about your general knowledge. You're involved in diplomatic service. You're a soldier in the army. The press and the news with regard to the fighting in Vukovar was something that would have been very important to you, to keep up to date with the diplomatic situation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I say I knew a bit more than the average Yugoslav did, and perhaps I was more interested in specifically that, zone because my mother hails from a village near Vukovar, old Kometinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You were aware that Vukovar was an important event, and you were aware that the Vukovar Hospital had become part of a cause celebre, if I can call it that, in the media both nationally and internationally; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I should like to assure the Trial Chamber that I knew less about that hospital and all the events surrounding it than about some other events. That hospital was referred to for the first time in my presence, as I stated in my previous answers, when I was in the compound of the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to your itinerary that day, can you just remind us who it was that drew up the itinerary, the actual stops that you had to go to with Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: The Deputy Federal Secretary for National Defence, Admiral Brovet, gave me a written itinerary with the indicated working points, as we call them, on route to Vukovar up to the return to our hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And that itinerary included stopping at Sid and then Negoslavci headquarters and then the Vukovar barracks and Velepromet; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and at the hospital in Negoslavci. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So the visit to Negoslavci hospital was also part of the original itinerary given to you on the 18th of November; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And Vukovar Hospital itself, the general hospital, was not included on that agenda, that itinerary; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Stojic, that Mr. Vance had expressly asked to go to Vukovar Hospital on the 18th of November, the day before you took him to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And any meeting between Mr. Vance and Admiral Brovet to draw up an agenda, you weren't at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, can you think of any reason why Vukovar Hospital would be kept off of the itinerary or agenda?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I would like to point out that we went to Negoslavci, as one of these most important points, where the command of Operations Group South was; that is to say, that we did not go to the command post of Operations Group North, on the other side of the Vuka River, where Major General Bjorcevic was commander. The hospital is not the in the zone of responsibility and combat activities. So it was not in the area of responsibility and combat activities of Operations Group South, but on the other side of the Vuka River, I think about four and a half to five kilometres away from barracks. So once I received my assignment to take the delegation to the command post, of course, including these working points like Sid, on route to the command post of Operations Group South, that is the zone outside the territory where the hospital was. Had Admiral Brovet ordered me to go on or to try to visit some other points, within the zone of responsibility of Operations Group North, I would have to know that; and I would then actually cooperate with the commander of Operations Group North, Major General Bjorcevic. However, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to Exhibit 70 and the video that you were shown earlier, showing Cyrus Vance and Major Sljivancanin at the barracks, and you described the conversation where Mr. Vance asks to go to the hospital, is it not the case that Mr. Sljivancanin refused to take Mr. Vance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: It is not the case that he refused. He said -- I mean, please, you can have a look at it again. He said that he thought that he could not organise a visit like that over the short term, that that's what he thought. I mean, please, of course this was 15 years ago. I have forgotten quite a bit. But thanks to the report that was submitted to me by Mr. Lukic during these days, in his office, and the footage I saw a while ago, and I saw it at Mr. Lukic's as well, you can see that Mr. Sljivancanin at that time is saying, "I think." He's not saying "I won't" or "I cannot."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard, then, to the excerpt from the video Exhibit 70, you're saying he's saying -- sorry, you've said that Sljivancanin was not saying "won't" or "cannot." But can we look, please, at the transcript of the video that was distributed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Now, the English is page 2, line 14. And there is a B/C/S version for the witness, if he would desire that, although I'll give him the English and the B/C/S for sake of completeness. If I could ask that to be given to the witness just now, Your Honour. From the English page -- before we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, are you happy to work from the English translation, given the level of your English influency?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can then look, please, at page 2, starting at line 7, you will see a request from Cyrus Vance asking to go to the hospital; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And at line 14, we have Major Sljivancanin's response: "I think I cannot ensure that at the moment." He is using the word "cannot," and he is disallowing any visit to the hospital at that stage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Only in part. May I explain? In our language, when somebody says "I think," that is the conditional; that is to say, that is what he thinks; that that is impossible due to the shortness of time and because he does not know what the situation was.
