On the other hand, even if the situation were 100 percent safe and secure, according to military regulations, one commander, rather, one unit cannot do something without previously reaching agreement on that activity with another unit that is responsible for that zone; that is to say, that on the assumption that even if one could have gone to the hospital and even if there had been enough time - let us disregard for the moment the fact that Mr. Vance was supposed to continue his very complicated journey via Grac to Zagreb, because he had meetings scheduled there - communication had to be established with the command of Group North. Even if the security situation were all right, that had to be agreed upon so time was required. When somebody says "I think, I cannot," in our language, that is the conditional; that is to say, something that he is not sure that he can do, that he thinks he cannot do; or, perhaps, some circumstances may prove to be helpful and change the situation into it actually being possible. I don't think that we can look upon this as a refusal on his part, only he is saying that he thinks he cannot. That is why, in my report, I stated the following sentence: "That in a well-augmented, well-founded fashion, an explanation was provided to Mr. Vance what the situation was regarding the hospital." I wrote my report a few hours after our return, trying to include each and every detail in order to know who did what and whether that was done properly, and who was responsible for what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, Mr. Stojic. Given that explanation -- rather, in spite of that explanation, Major Sljivancanin did not take any steps to see if the visit to the hospital was possible, nor did he make any inquiries to see if a visit to the hospital was possible; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That's not the way it was exactly. Quite simply, Mr. Cyrus Vance did not really insist very much. I claim that with responsibility. He asked two or three times, but -- I mean, I was following everything that was going on, but I started thinking --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Stojic, the question was: Did --

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Stojic, did Major Sljivancanin make any inquiries about going to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that, whether he was making any inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojic, you were asked about a rifle being pointed at Mr. Vance by Major Sljivancanin. The Prosecution does not accept the position you've given. Is it not the case that Mr. Sljivancanin did, indeed, raise a rifle towards Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That is not true. That is absolutely untrue. He didn't even have a rifle, by the way. And even if that had been the case, it would have figured very prominently in my report. And also, all the media, all the world media and our media, would have presented that as breaking news in their headlines. If somebody points a rifle at someone, then they do not really shake hands; whereas, when they parted, Mr. Vance shook hands with him and they said goodbye quite normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to that report you've mentioned, Exhibit 861 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I wonder if we can have that on the screens, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your report, Mr. Stojic, would have been prepared carefully, and you wanted it to be accurate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor please switch off the microphone when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If Mr. Vance had said anything that you did not agree with, you would have had the opportunity to refer to that in this report, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And can we please look at page 2 of the English version and page 3 of the B/C/S version of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You reported, Mr. Stojic, that Cyrus Vance had stressed that the volunteers and the territorial units "are behaving in a manner somewhat unfit for a soldier, and they should be put under control as soon as possible." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I recall that, because I saw it the other day. When speaking to Mr. Lukic, I was reminded of that. I saw that report a few days ago here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Stojic, that by using the word "behaving," it conveys that the TO and volunteers were doing something actively to be seen to be unfit for soldiers, rather than just standing and the way they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: He probably thought that if someone was attired in an unsoldierly way, that that person was prepared to do something that was not in accordance with regulations. But now I cannot say whether that was exactly what he meant. He saw, on the approaches to the barracks; that is to say, outside the compound - and I saw it, too, because I was with him all the time - a few armed members whose attire showed that they did not belong to the operative part of the Yugoslav People's Army. He probably thought that these people would be capable of doing something that was not in accordance with military regulations. That is why I mentioned that in my report, so that my superiors would be prepared to talk about this and take certain measures to resolve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can move on, please, Mr. Stojic, to the meeting between Cyrus Vance and General Kadijevic after your return from Vukovar. Can I suggest to you that at that meeting, the one you've described, that contrary to your evidence this morning, Mr. Vance was furious at the treatment he had received from Major Sljivancanin, and he was furious about the general treatment from the JNA; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That is untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Is it not the case that Mr. Vance told General Kadijevic that whilst he was in Vukovar, he had been obstructed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Is it not the case that Mr. Vance told General Kadijevic that there were physical efforts to intimidate him whilst he was in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That is not the case. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And is it not true that Mr. Vance told General Kadijevic that whilst he was in Vukovar, the JNA had been telling him falsehoods and telling him lies.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, are you sure you were at this meeting between Mr. Vance and General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: When such meetings were held, I would definitely attend, and I was definitely present on that day. But I do have to say that the protocol office that I was head of does not take direct part in the talks at the table. We have -- we had four of our representatives sitting at the table; General Kadijevic, with the four officials who were mentioned already. The recording clerk keeps minutes at a separate table. All the while, I'm there, waiting, standing by, listening, and waiting for orders as to what I should do further. In such an activity, such a visit, the chief of the administration, or rather, the liaison office is definitely always involved. And, in view of the fact that I had compiled -- that I have to write a report, that they were discussing -- that they also had my report, it was logical that I should be there, because they could have asked me questions in relation to that report, to what I had put in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit 68, Your Honours, and in particular, page 3 of the four-page exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, do you now see that in front of you on the screen, a handwritten document with two pages?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, that is the diary of Herbert Okun, Ambassador Okun, and we've heard evidence that he made contemporaneous notes during the course of this delegation, this trip to Belgrade, to Vukovar, and so forth. If we look at the left-hand page of page 3, it's got "92" in the top left corner. Do you see "92?"

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do see 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And it would appear, Mr. Stojic, wouldn't it, that this was a meeting in Belgrade on 21st November of 1991, at 2 p.m. to 2.50 p.m., and it lists a number of names there, which includes General Kadijevic and next to the letters UN, "CRV." Now, you've heard evidence that "CRV" is Cyrus Vance. This is a record from Mr. Okun as to who was at the meeting. Your name is on that list anywhere, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No. It is not, but can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The question was: Was your name on it? And your answer was no. If my learned friend wants to clear up anything in re-examination, he may do so. But your name is not on that list; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And we'll see further down the page, about halfway down the left-hand page, the words "matters of concern;" and two lines before that, "increased violence, Vukovar, disproportionate use of force at Vuk". Now, is it the case that Mr. Vance was at the clear at that meeting, and he clearly told General Kadijevic that he was unhappy with the situation in Vukovar and he was unhappy with his treatment at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: It is not true that he said anything about not having been treated well during his visit to Vukovar. Actually, that was not discussed at all. And as regards these names, if you will allow me, they stated the party participating in the conversation. General Jovic, the ex-commander of the United Nations, is the person whom I replaced, General Slavko Jovic. Then the protocol, the typist, the steno clerk, the recording service, they are sitting on the side and recording the minutes, and I was in charge of that particular activity. I was not participating in the talks. Everybody's place was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to the next page in the exhibit, page 4, which has "96" -- the number "96" in the top left-hand corner and the number "97" in the top right-hand corner. Do you see that document, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Or that page, rather.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And there seems to be on the right-hand page, page 97, next to the entry "3.35 p.m. to 4.30 p.m." reference to a meeting between Cyrus Vance and the late President Slobodan Milosevic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You weren't present for that meeting, were you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If Your Honour would allow me for one minute, there's one question I want to ask, but I have to confer with my learned friend next to me. If Your Honour would allow me a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, one more question, Mr. Stojic, and just to go back to your briefing with Colonel Mrksic. Were you never told that -- rather, strike that. Were you told that OG South had been asked to take the hospital on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And that that was to be completed by the morning of the 19th of November at 10 a.m. No one told you that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: I assert with full responsibility, before this honourable Trial Chamber, that not even Mr. Lukic mentioned that to me. And this is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lunny. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we can immediately proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic, had Mr. Vance insisted that he visit the hospital at Vukovar, could Major Sljivancanin have prevented you from taking Mr. Vance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No, he could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that there were a lot of journalists there. Mr. Lunny also asked you about them. In the days that followed, if you had occasion at all to follow the media reports, did you see in any media source, either domestic or foreign press, that any incidents during Mr. Vance's visit to Vukovar was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny showed you your report in which you put certain remarks by Mr. Vance which he gave to you when you were returning home, including those related to the territorials, and those objections of his were inserted in your report.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had Mr. Vance voiced any assertions about things that were not part of your report to General Kadijevic, what would have been the consequences for you personally, as the person who compiled the report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: It was my task to monitor, to follow, everything else closely and to draw up a very objective report, in order for General Kadijevic, with his associates, to be able to prepare themselves for the conversation and to know what needed to be undertaken to resolve problems, if any. I wrote that report, as you know, for several hours after returning to Belgrade, when this august Tribunal hadn't even been set up, when we didn't know how events would actually evolve. So my intention was to write an objective report and to include in it everything which was of consequence during that visit, which was material. If there had been anything that I omitted to include in my report and had happened, not only would I have been replaced, but I would have borne more difficult consequences, quite probably; not to mention that in a way, I, as you well know, Mr. Lukic, was a part of that military top leadership. Truth to tell, not in its operational segment. I have referred to my role in the protocol a number of times. So I would have been lying to myself had I produced an untruthful report. Apart from that, I did not know Major Sljivancanin at all. I came to know him much better later than then. So if you ask me, during that visit, Mr. Sljivancanin does speak in a loud voice, whether he is at a party or carrying out a task, but that certainly could not be seen or lead to a conclusion that he was impertinent. Now, as regards your question whether he could have prevented him, had Mr. Cyrus Vance insisted to go to the hospital, although that would have been complicated because of the shortness of time, because of his trip, because the hospital was in the zone of another group, of another operations group, Group North, I would have called Admiral Brovet, in that case, and briefed him of the newly emerged situation for him to make a decision as to what we should be -- what we should do. In that case, General Kadijevic would have ordered the commander of the Operations Group South how to proceed; and, thereby, my own responsibility would have ended. As that didn't happen, I described the entire sequence of events in my report as they unfolded, endeavouring in the process to include in it everything which is relevant and to portray a picture for General Kadijevic and his associates of how everything had transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that that is clear. Did you want to append any further explanations? But we do want to be concise.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: If you have a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny also asked you whether you had seen Mr. Sljivancanin make any further inquiries, whether it was possible to go to the hospital, and you said that he didn't. So I'm asking you this: After your talk with Mr. Vance, did he ever again voice a wish to go and see the hospital? But just be brief.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: And to tell you something, I was relieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: Because I would have had to call Admiral Brovet; and you know something, it wasn't all that simple. It was 4.5 kilometres off. The hospital was downtown in the center, and I would have had to use the stairs, and so on and so forth. I don't want to dwell much upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Just another topic, very briefly. Mr. Lunny showed you Mr. Okun's log, where your name is not mentioned as being present at a meeting with Mr. Kadijevic. And he states that he -- he submits that you were not, in fact, present at that meeting, and you explained how it had been. My question is different. There is no need for you to look at every page. Mr. Lunny can also confirm this. Your name is not mentioned either when you went to Vukovar, so I am going to ask you this: Did you go to Vukovar on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR STOJIC
utterances.text: You saw me on the footage; and also it may be of interest to note that I hosted a dinner for Mr. Okun and the delegation at the army centre of Yugoslavia, after this meeting in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and we had a very good time, especially with Mr. Purola, with Mr. Purola and Okun. And as for the rifle --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no need to comment further on this point. Mr. Stojic, I have no further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you will be glad to know that that concludes the questions that are to be asked of you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here and your assistance, and you, of course, are now free to go back to your ordinary affairs. Thank you very much. The court officer will take you out. Sorry, you were wanting to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is an honour and privilege for me to have had this opportunity to be acquainted with this honourable Trial Chamber. I thank you very much for the fair treatment accorded to me on the part of all the parties in this august Tribunal. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank all my colleagues and my adversaries for having dealt with this witness expeditiously, and even faster than we had envisaged. So for the first time, our Defence team is in a situation of not having a witness to call. Perhaps we could have rested a bit more last week instead of working so quickly. So we will be calling our next witness on Monday, according to our schedule, as announced. I apologise. Mr. Karanfilov will be our next witness on Monday, as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we appreciate the position, and it will we necessary, therefore, to adjourn early today, to resume on Monday, I think it is at 2.15 on Monday. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
